A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEP study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v2 Appendices A–D to v3 and inspecting the new Appendix E.

before.justification: v2 reports original separation and utility measurements for nine language models, mitigation experiments, failure cases, and analyses by dataset attributes.

after.justification: v3 retains original model evaluations and reports additional SFT, DPO, mixed-data training, and combined prompt-engineering/fine-tuning results.

M1.justification: The mitigation procedures expand from supervised LoRA fine-tuning to include mixed-data SFT targeting separation and utility, DPO using probe/no-probe response pairs, and fine-tuning with the strongest prompt template. Appendix B.4 also changes LoRA targets from including embeddings to excluding them. The empirical witness-based scoring procedure remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds Guanaco instruction-tuning data for mixed training and replaces the introductory translation demonstration with an email/API simulation. SEP's 9,160 examples and task inventory remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 names SEP as a training-mixture component, conflicting with Section 4's evaluation-only restriction; actual overlap cannot be established.

E2.justification: v3 adds DPO and balanced SFT to the fine-tuning comparison and compares SFT/DPO combined with prompt engineering on three models (Tables 11–12 and 17–18). The nine-model main comparison is retained. Appendix E evaluates a StruQ-inspired combination, rather than documenting a separate reproduction of StruQ itself.

E3.justification: The reported fine-tuning schedule changes from constant learning rate with warm-up to cosine with warm-up (v2 Table 10; v3 Table 13), and embedding adaptation is excluded. Added experiments specify a 50:50 data mixture and combined-template training on three models. SEP size, empirical metrics, and the stated three-epoch budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Balanced SFT tests whether adding ordinary instruction-tuning data preserves utility, while new Appendix E tests whether combining the best prompt template with SFT or DPO improves separation. These substantially extend the mitigation analysis. Existing insistence, position, domain, and GPT failure-case analyses are retained; Figure 1 replaces the translation case with an email/API failure.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting becomes less uniform: v2 Table 4 reports standard errors for SFT utility, whereas v3 Table 12 presents revised SFT and balanced-SFT utilities as point estimates; Table 18 also omits utility uncertainty. Main tables retain standard errors. Neither version reports repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Original/Naive and prompt-based results remain unchanged, but fine-tuning results are replaced and expanded. For example, Phi-3 separation/utility changes from 27.7%/1.5% under v2 SFT to 97.0%/69.2% under v3 DPO; this is not a same-setting improvement. New training and combination results appear in Tables 11–12 and 17–18. v3 inconsistently reports average DPO separation as 95.5% in Table 4 and 96.0% in Table 11.

T1.justification: Definition 1 explicitly limits the abstraction to single-turn models. Definition 2 replaces the fixed KL divergence with a general distributional dissimilarity, mentioning KL and Wasserstein, and reverses the displayed argument order. Surprise-witness and empirical separation/utility definitions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement narrow the formal contribution to single-turn models. Section 6.1 softens the conjecture that separation will require fundamentally new approaches to saying it will benefit from them. The central contributions—formal characterization, SEP, and empirical evidence of inadequate separation—remain.

C2.justification: v3 introduces task superposition as a hypothesis for why larger models execute both instructions and probes. It interprets revised fine-tuning results as reducing usefulness for some tasks, replacing v2's stronger statement that many resulting models are no longer useful. Training data and scale are added as possible explanations for GPT performance.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly documents DPOTrainer, disabling LoRA adapters for reference-model passes, the 50:50 Guanaco mixture, and equal-step learning-rate searches. Table 13 adds 40 warm-up steps and DPO beta 0.1. Hardware, most existing hyperparameters, and code/data access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially expand coverage of RAG and agentic prompt injection, instruction hierarchy, activation-based detection, and data-minimization defenses. Added works include AgentDojo, ConfusedPilot, Wallace et al., Abdelnabi et al., and Bagdasarian et al. The earlier five-part differentiation is replaced by positioning centered on isolating instruction-data separation from attacks and harmful-query safety.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten around email/API and RAG applications. Metric exposition and the fine-tuning discussion are revised, Original is renamed Naive, and Appendix E is added. The main section sequence and much of the dataset and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adopts ICLR formatting, changing headers, typography, text widths, and table placement throughout. Figure 1 becomes a full-width colored email/API example, and Figure 2 is rescaled and updated. New Tables 11–12 and 17–18 display expanded experiments; Table 2 redisplays an existing prompt template. Existing failure-case and dataset-breakdown tables are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The additional training-objective and combined-mitigation comparisons strengthen evidence beyond v2's single fine-tuning approach, while explicit single-turn scope and a softer architectural-necessity claim improve calibration. These gains are limited by conflicting descriptions of SEP's role in training and inconsistent DPO summaries across Tables 4 and 11, which weaken confidence in parts of the expanded evidence.
